title: fix(hardware): prevent ~130s sleep wake stall on MacBook Pro 2016-2017
author: tcholewa
body:
### Summary

Fixes a ~130-second system freeze on wake from ACPI S3 (`deep`) sleep on MacBook Pro 2016–2017 models (MacBookPro13,x and MacBookPro14,x).

### Root Cause
On MacBook Pro 2016–2017 models equipped with Intel Alpine Ridge Thunderbolt 3 controllers (`8086:15d2` NHI / `8086:15d4` integrated xHCI), Apple firmware cuts power to the controller during S3 sleep. On wake, `xhci_hcd` polls the unpowered PCIe device (`0000:07:00.0`), hitting exponential backoff timeouts (`1023ms` -> `2047ms` -> ... -> `65535ms`) totalling ~130 seconds before `pciehp` drops the dead device.

### Solution
1. Adds `install/hardware/apple/fix-suspend-thunderbolt.sh` to remove unpowered `8086:15d4` PCIe devices prior to S3 sleep.
2. Unloads `thunderbolt` and `facetimehd` before sleep to prevent kernel call traces and unneeded sensor power-on.
3. Automatically dispatches `hl.dsp.dpms({ action = "enable" })` upon resume across active Hyprland user sessions so the display backlight lights up immediately.
4. Rescans the Thunderbolt root port (`0000:00:1c.4`) after resume.
5. Updates `manual/44-mac-support.md` with documentation.

files.patch:
@@ -0,0 +1,49 @@
+# Fix Thunderbolt/xHCI sleep stall on MacBook Pro models (2016-2017)
+# In ACPI S3 sleep, Apple firmware cuts power to the Alpine Ridge controller (8086:15d2/15d4).
+# Removing the unpowered xHCI controller before sleep prevents xhci_hcd from freezing for ~130s on wake.
+macbook_model=$(cat /sys/class/dmi/id/product_name 2>/dev/null || true)
+
+if [[ $macbook_model =~ MacBookPro13,[123]|MacBookPro14,[123] ]]; then
+  echo "Detected MacBook Pro with Alpine Ridge Thunderbolt ($macbook_model)"
+  echo "Applying Thunderbolt and display sleep fixes..."
+
+  sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system-sleep
+  sudo tee /etc/systemd/system-sleep/omarchy-macbook-sleep.sh >/dev/null <<'EOF'
+#!/bin/bash
+case "$1/$2" in
+  pre/*)
+    for dev in /sys/bus/pci/devices/*; do
+      if [[ -f "$dev/vendor" && -f "$dev/device" ]]; then
+        if [[ $(cat "$dev/vendor" 2>/dev/null) == "0x8086" && $(cat "$dev/device" 2>/dev/null) == "0x15d4" ]]; then
+          echo 1 > "$dev/remove" 2>/dev/null || true
+        fi
+      fi
+    done
+    [[ -d /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:07:00.0 ]] && echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:07:00.0/remove 2>/dev/null || true
+
+    [[ -d /sys/module/thunderbolt ]] && modprobe -r thunderbolt 2>/dev/null || true
+    [[ -d /sys/module/facetimehd ]] && modprobe -r facetimehd 2>/dev/null || true
+    ;;
+
+  post/*)
+    for user_dir in /run/user/*; do
+      if [[ -d "$user_dir/hypr" ]]; then
+        uid=$(basename "$user_dir")
+        uname=$(id -nu "$uid" 2>/dev/null)
+        sig=$(ls -td "$user_dir/hypr/"* 2>/dev/null | head -1 | xargs basename 2>/dev/null)
+        if [[ -n "$uname" && -n "$sig" ]]; then
+          ( runuser -u "$uname" -- env XDG_RUNTIME_DIR="$user_dir" HYPRLAND_INSTANCE_SIGNATURE="$sig" hyprctl dispatch 'hl.dsp.dpms({ action = "enable" })' >/dev/null 2>&1 || true ) &
+        fi
+      fi
+    done
+
+    [[ -d /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:00:1c.4 ]] && ( sleep 2 && echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:00:1c.4/rescan ) >/dev/null 2>&1 &
+    ;;
+esac
+EOF
+
+  sudo chmod 755 /etc/systemd/system-sleep/omarchy-macbook-sleep.sh
+
+  sudo mkdir -p /etc/modprobe.d
+  echo "blacklist thunderbolt" | sudo tee /etc/modprobe.d/disable-thunderbolt.conf >/dev/null
+fi

comments.body:
Tested this on a **MacBookPro14,1** (Omarchy 4.0.2, systemd 261.2, kernel 7.1.9-arch1-2). The diagnosis matches what I see here, and with the hook actually running the xHCI backoff and the `tb_cfg_read` trace disappear and the USB-C ports survive sleep.

Worth noting this is not covered by `fix-suspend-nvme.sh`: that service was installed and applied (`d3cold_allowed=0`) on a machine that still hung hard on resume from S3 and needed a power cycle.

Three notes on the patch as written — the first prevented it from running on my system.

### 1. The hook directory isn't scanned on systemd 261

`fix-suspend-thunderbolt.sh` writes to `/etc/systemd/system-sleep/`. On systemd 261.2 that directory doesn't appear to be searched: `systemd-sleep(8)` documents only `/usr/lib/systemd/system-sleep/`, and that's the only such path in the shipped binaries:

```console
$ strings /usr/lib/systemd/systemd-sleep /usr/lib/systemd/libsystemd-shared-261.2-1.so \
    | grep -o '[/A-Za-z0-9._-]*system-sleep[/A-Za-z0-9._-]*' | sort -u
/usr/lib/systemd/system-sleep
```

With the script in `/etc/...` the hook silently never ran here — the xHCI was still present going into S3, and resume showed the full backoff plus a call trace:

```
xhci_hcd 0000:07:00.0: not ready 1023ms after resume; waiting
  ... 2047 / 4095 / 8191 / 16383 / 32767 ...
xhci_hcd 0000:07:00.0: not ready 65535ms after resume; giving up
thunderbolt 0000:06:00.0: not ready 1023ms after resume; giving up
WARNING: drivers/thunderbolt/ctl.c:1131 at tb_cfg_read+0x94/0xf0 [thunderbolt]
```

Moving the identical script to `/usr/lib/systemd/system-sleep/` fixed it — those messages and the `tb_cfg_read` trace both went to zero, and the USB-C ports survived sleep instead of staying dead until reboot. That's also where the repo's existing `unmount-fuse` hook already lives, so it may be worth matching it regardless of which systemd versions searched `/etc`.

### 2. The `dpms` dispatch blocks resume for ~5.4s

systemd keeps `user.slice` frozen until every `post` hook returns, so the `runuser ... hyprctl dispatch` call delays the session coming back:

```
04:15:33.128  post hook starts
04:15:33.140  runuser session opened
04:15:33.199  systemd: Cannot start frozen unit Session 3 of User <user>.
04:15:33.200  pam_systemd: CreateSession failed: io.systemd.Login.UnitAllocationFailed
04:15:38.530  runuser session closed          <- 5.33s
04:15:40.617  user.slice thawed
```

Note pam fails immediately (60 ms) — the 5.33s is `hyprctl` waiting on a Hyprland that is itself frozen and cannot reply. `systemd-sleep(8)` warns about precisely this:

> user.slice will be frozen while the executables are running, so they should not attempt to communicate with any user services expecting a reply.

This repo's own `unmount-fuse` hook already documents the hazard and backgrounds its work for that reason.

The dispatch also wasn't necessary here — ACPI restores the panel on its own (`acpi LNXVIDEO:00: Restoring backlight state`). Dropping it, and making the `sleep 2` + rescan conditional, took the frozen window from **7.49s to 0.057s** across two otherwise identical sleep cycles:

```
suspend exit -> user.slice thawed
  with dpms + unconditional sleep 2 : 7.490s
  without                           : 0.057s
```

The unconditional `sleep 2` before the rescan is likewise unnecessary on the happy path: after a clean pre-removal the xHCI re-enumerates by itself, so the rescan only earns its keep as a fallback.

### 3. The hardcoded `0000:07:00.0` removal is redundant and risky

```bash
[[ -d /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:07:00.0 ]] && echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:07:00.0/remove 2>/dev/null || true
```

The loop above it already removes every `8086:15d4`. On this machine `07:00.0` *is* that device, so the line is a no-op; on other hardware that address can be an unrelated device, which would then be removed before every suspend. Suggest dropping it.

### A data point supporting the approach

Once a resume has wedged the controller it cannot be recovered without a power cycle — I tried rescanning the root port, the xHCI's immediate parent bridge (`0000:05:02.0`), and a global `/sys/bus/pci/rescan`, and none brought it back. That supports the PR's core premise of removing the device *before* firmware cuts power rather than trying to restore it afterwards.

Minor: `blacklist thunderbolt` in `/etc/modprobe.d` disables Thunderbolt devices entirely. Since the `pre` hook already unloads the module, reloading it in `post` instead keeps docks/eGPU usable while awake and still avoids the NHI traces.

Hi @tcholewa, @ari-ahm — I've been chasing exactly this failure on a MacBookPro14,1 for the last two weeks and I think it's worth cross-linking, because we ended up at a different diagnosis and a different fix. The log signature you both posted (`xhci_hcd 0000:07:00.0: not ready 1023ms … 65535ms after resume; giving up`, `thunderbolt 0000:06:00.0: not ready 1023ms`, the `tb_cfg_read` WARNING at `ctl.c:1131`) is line-for-line what I captured on the stock kernel, so it is the same bug.

Write-up: #10593. Patches: omacom/omarchy-pkgs#349 (`tb-ar-shim-dkms`, the kernel-side fix) and #10758 (detection, install and a migration that depend on it).

### Root cause is a PCI save-ordering hazard, not a firmware power cut

Instrumented on the machine (config-space reads from a shim module at each PM phase):

1. `dpm_suspend_noirq` runs children before parents. The NHI (`06:00.0`) is the deepest child, and its `nhi_suspend_noirq → tb_switch_suspend → tb_lc_set_sleep` puts the Alpine Ridge router into LC sleep. From that moment config reads of *the whole chip* — the downstream bridges **and the upstream bridge `04:00.0`** — return `ffffffff`. (This is the "Unable to change power state from D0 to D3hot, device inaccessible" trio on 05:02.0 / 05:00.0 / 04:00.0 in the stock suspend log.)
2. Only after that does `pci_pm_suspend_noirq` run for the bridges and call `pci_save_state()`. It saves all-ones.
3. Across S3 the platform resets and re-powers the chip on its own — the rails are up and RP05's link is retrained to Gen3 x4 before the first noirq resume callback. Nothing needs to (or does) cut power.
4. `pci_pm_resume_noirq(04:00.0)` restores the all-ones snapshot into the fresh chip: bus numbers `ff`, so every downstream bridge is "inaccessible", the NHI's `pci_dev_wait` gives up after 1 s, the xHCI's after 65 s, and pciehp removes it. That is the ~130 s.

For S3, saving the bridge and its subtree in `suspend_late` — i.e. before the NHI's noirq callback — is the entire fix. With that alone, resume of the subtree takes 1.3 s and the NHI, the Thunderbolt domain and the xHCI all survive. (Under s2idle there is a second, mirror-image bug: the PCI core's `skip_bus_pm` policy skips the restore entirely, on the assumption that devices keep their config space across s2idle, which this chip doesn't. So the module also has to do the parents-first restore itself in `resume_noirq`.) 28/28 cycles on 14,1 with both in place.

A supporting data point: **hibernate works on the stock kernel.** The thunderbolt driver's `freeze_noirq` deliberately does not LC-sleep ("we just disable hotplug, the pci-tunnels stay alive"), so the snapshot that goes into the image is valid, and restore writes it back into the cold-reset chip. That is the same ordering the shim manufactures for S3.

### Why this hook works, and what it costs

`modprobe -r thunderbolt` in the pre hook means `tb_lc_set_sleep` is never called, so the core's own `pci_save_state()` in noirq sees a readable chip. That is the operative line; the `remove` of the `15d4` xHCI is most likely redundant once the NHI driver is gone. The cost is that `blacklist thunderbolt` disables Thunderbolt for good — docks, tunneled PCIe, eGPUs — and, as @ari-ahm found, even the reload-in-post variant keeps the driver off for the whole sleep window.

### The second failure mode this hook does not reach

There is a separate, worse failure that only happens when **something is physically present on a Thunderbolt port at S3 entry**: the Mac's EFI S3 resume boot script function-disables the PCH root port `00:1c.4` (RP05) itself, ~4–6 ms after "Waking up from system sleep state S3" and before the kernel runs a single instruction. RP05 reads `ffffffff` from then on and nothing short of a power cycle brings it back — rescanning the root port, its parent, and a global `/sys/bus/pci/rescan` all do nothing. Reproduced 8/8; we eliminated 11 OS-side countermeasures one at a time (wake-source disarming, D-state pinning, driver unbinding, link-state forcing, PD-controller mailbox commands, …). Unbinding the xHCI driver before suspend in particular does *not* help: the SuperSpeed link stays trained at U0 with nothing bound, and it is physical presence, not the driver, that trips the firmware. I'd expect `echo 1 > remove` to behave the same. @ari-ahm's "still hung hard on resume from S3 and needed a power cycle" looks like this mode.

Since s2idle never executes the EFI S3 boot script, that firmware behaviour cannot fire at all — which is why #10758 defaults these models to `mem_sleep_default=s2idle` via a limine cmdline drop-in. That is an honest trade: s2idle draws more in the bag than S3 does (no firmware S0ix assist on this platform). In exchange, both failure modes are gone (validated with a hub + stick attached, lid-close with Wi-Fi loaded, and cold-boot persistence), and Thunderbolt keeps working. macOS clearly slept in S3 with devices attached, so there is presumably a pre-sleep handshake it performs that we haven't found; that is the open research item in the issue.

### Scope notes

- The DKMS module is ~200 lines and gates on the on-board controller only (ACPI path `DSB0.NHI0.SXFP` under the bridge). The in-tree version is being prepared as a `drivers/pci/quirks.c` fixup for linux-pci; module, patch and CI live at https://github.com/orospakr/linux-apple-alpine-ridge-suspend.
- I've only validated on MacBookPro14,1. The mechanism should be identical on 13,x/14,2/14,3 (same DSL6540 controller, same ACPI shape), but I haven't had one to test.

Happy to compare notes or logs — the full account, including the experiments that ruled things out, is in the issue. If the project would rather ship a hook-based workaround in the short term, the one-line takeaway from the above is that unloading `thunderbolt` is what makes it work, and the SS-device-attached case still needs s2idle.
